42860780.label: Objective
42860780.text: Motion artifacts remain a limitation of cardiac CT when assessing both native and prosthetic heart valves, particularly during phases of rapid motion. This may lead to reduced image quality, potentially impairing the evaluation of valvular movement and pathology. The purpose of this study was to evaluate whether a novel reconstruction-based motion correction algorithm improves image quality and reduces motion artifacts of native and prosthetic heart valves compared with standard reconstructions in photon-counting detector CT (PCD-CT).

42860780.label: Materials and methods
42860780.text: In this retrospective single-center study, 57 patients [21 women; median age, 71 (interquartile range, 57 to 78 y)] who underwent clinically indicated 4D cardiac CT for suspected native and prosthetic valvular disease were included. Images were acquired using retrospectively electrocardiography (ECG)-gated spiral dual-source PCD-CT without ECG-pulsing. Images were reconstructed in 10% steps throughout the RR-interval using both standard (TrueStack) and an otherwise identical reconstruction using the novel motion correction algorithm (ZeeFreePlus). Subjective image quality and motion artifacts were independently assessed by 2 blinded, experienced readers using a 4-point visual analog scale for 3 categories: valve frame/annulus, valve leaflets, and valvular pathology. Objective analysis included quantification of the volume of artifacts throughout the cardiac cycle.

42860780.label: Results
42860780.text: A total of 68 valves were evaluated, including 57 prosthetic valves (22 transcatheter aortic valve replacements and 19 surgical valves, 11 mitral valves, and 5 tricuspid valve interventions) and 11 native valves. Valvular pathology was present in 29 cases, with the most prevalent being hypoattenuated leaflet thickening in 14/29 (48%). Motion-corrected reconstructions significantly improved image quality and reduced motion artifacts across all cardiac phases and all categories (all, P <0.001). The largest improvements were observed during systole, particularly at 10% of the RR-interval, with significantly greater gains than during diastole ( P <0.05). Improvements were consistent across aortic and atrioventricular prosthetic valves and translated into improved visualization of valvular pathology ( P <0.001). Objective quantitative analysis corroborated the subjective image quality findings by demonstrating reductions in the volumes of motion-induced artifacts when using the algorithm ( P <0.001).

42860780.label: Conclusions
42860780.text: A novel motion correction algorithm substantially reduced motion artifacts and improved image quality in both native and prosthetic heart valve imaging with PCD-CT, with the largest improvements in systole. These benefits resulted in enhanced visualization of valvular pathology, potentially reinforcing the growing clinical role of cardiac CT for the assessment of valve disease.

42862280.label: Objective
42862280.text: Pre-therapy blood-marrow dosimetry for ¹³¹I treatment of differentiated thyroid cancer (DTC) requires serial imaging and blood sampling, limiting clinical adoption. When blood data are unavailable, operators fall back to fixed or imaging-only prescribing, usually without an explicit uncertainty bound. We characterise the cohort electron blood self-dose fraction (βfrac) in a single-centre ¹²⁴I PET cohort and quantify the uncertainty incurred by substituting that reference for patient-specific blood data.

42862280.label: Methods
42862280.text: Retrospective single-centre analysis of 18 pre-therapy ¹²⁴I PET courses in 15 DTC patients with paired serial venous blood-counting, all prepared by thyroid-hormone withdrawal. Time-activity curves were fitted in the ¹³¹I therapy frame following the EANM Standard Operational Procedure, separating Dblood into its electron (β, blood self-dose) and photon (γ, body cross-fire) components. The substitution uncertainty was propagated analytically, then validated against patient-level errors by leave-one-patient-out cross-validation.

42862280.label: Results
42862280.text: The cohort β fraction was 84.3 ± 4.8% across 18 courses (mean ± SD; median 85.4%; 95% CI 82.0-86.7%), and 84.4 ± 4.6% over the 15 patients. The β fraction decreased with body weight (- 0.113 pp/kg, p = 0.019), although not significantly when reduced to one value per patient (p = 0.118); the association is therefore exploratory. Substitution gave a per-patient 1-σ uncertainty on the imaging-only Dblood estimate of ≈ 30%. Under leave-one-patient-out cross-validation the mean absolute percentage error was 26.3% and the RMSE 32.7%, with 12 of 18 courses within ± 30% of their reference.

42862280.label: Conclusions
42862280.text: A cohort β fraction of 84.3 ± 4.8% is proposed as a fall-back reference for blood-free prescribing in DTC radioiodine therapy. Because the estimator's error is multiplicative on the estimate, a prescribing cap must come from the lower tail of that error, giving approximately 1.0-1.2 Gy in this cohort. No 95% coverage is demonstrated at this sample size, and the cap is offered as an exploratory observation requiring local confirmation rather than a validated threshold. The decomposition is imaging-modality agnostic for ¹³¹I clearance studies and therefore potentially applicable to low-dose ¹³¹I SPECT, although no SPECT data were analysed here.

42909580.label: Background
42909580.text: Bone scintigraphy using [99mTc]Tc-DPD or [99mTc]Tc-HMDP is a non-invasive cornerstone for diagnosing transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis (ATTR-CA). However, their interchangeability and the clinical relevance of systemic extracardiac uptake (ExtCU) remain poorly defined.

42909580.label: Aim
42909580.text: To systematically compare the diagnostic performance and whole-body biodistribution profiles of [99mTc]Tc-DPD and [99mTc]Tc-HMDP in patients with suspected cardiac amyloidosis (CA).

42909580.label: Methods
42909580.text: We retrospectively evaluated a multicenter cohort of patients investigated for suspected CA who underwent late planar whole-body scintigraphy and targeted SPECT/CT with either radiotracer as part of their diagnostic workup. Inclusion required a final, confirmed diagnosis of ATTRwt, ATTRv, or AL amyloidosis. Myocardial visual Perugini score (VISUAL_PS) and systemic ExtCU (pulmonary, appendicular muscular, visceral, and miscellaneous) were recorded.

42909580.label: Results
42909580.text: The study included 224 patients (DPD: n = 109, comprising 70 ATTRwt, 20 ATTRv, 19 AL; HMDP: n = 115, comprising 90 ATTRwt, 13 ATTRv, 12 AL). In ATTRwt, the DPD cohort presented predominantly with Perugini Grade 2 (76%), whereas the HMDP cohort skewed toward Grade 3 (72%, p < 0.001). DPD was significantly associated with appendicular muscular uptake (ATTRwt: 84% vs. 38%, p < 0.001), creating a competitive "soft-tissue sink effect". Conversely, HMDP demonstrated a unique predilection for pulmonary retention (ATTRwt: 68% vs. 46%, p = 0.008; ATTRv: 61% vs. 10%, p = 0.006). Visceral uptake was rare in ATTR but was a robust negative predictor strongly favoring AL amyloidosis (OR 0.016, p < 0.001).

42909580.label: Conclusions
42909580.text: [99mTc]Tc-DPD and [99mTc]Tc-HMDP possess distinct biodistribution profiles precluding direct interchangeability. HMDP maximizes myocardial contrast, whereas DPD provides a superior representation of the systemic musculoskeletal amyloid burden. Nuclear medicine physicians must adopt tracer-specific interpretive approaches to optimize non-invasive phenotyping.

42912580.text: Neuroblastoma (NB) is the most common extracranial solid malignancy of childhood, arising from neural crest cells of the sympathetic nervous system. Metastatic spread most frequently involves the bone marrow, bones, lymph nodes, and liver, whereas soft-tissue, central nervous system, and pulmonary metastases are less common. Unusual sites of recurrence may present a significant diagnostic challenge. We report a rare case of thymic relapse of NB presenting as an anterior mediastinal mass with intense uptake on 123 I-meta-iodobenzylguanidine ( 123 I-mIBG) scintigraphy. This case highlights an uncommon pattern of NB recurrence and the value of 123 I-mIBG imaging in its detection.

42914180.text: Uterine serous carcinoma (USC) is an aggressive endometrial cancer frequently associated with human epidermal growth factor receptor type 2 (HER2) overexpression and poor prognosis. Although trastuzumab improves outcomes, resistance remains a major clinical problem. This study determined whether targeted α-therapy using 211At-labeled trastuzumab (211At-trastuzumab) can overcome trastuzumab resistance in HER2-positive USC. Methods: 211At-trastuzumab was synthesized, and its binding and cytotoxicity in HER2-positive USC cell lines were evaluated. Three trastuzumab-resistant peritoneal metastasis mouse models were established: intrinsic resistance, trastuzumab-induced resistance, and acquired resistance. After a single intravenous administration (1.85 MBq), therapeutic efficacy was assessed using bioluminescence imaging and biodistribution analysis. Results: 211At-trastuzumab showed specific binding to HER2-positive USC cells and significantly reduced cell viability relative to the controls. In vivo, tumor uptake reached 17.4 ± 1.9 %ID/g at 24 h. A single dose significantly suppressed tumor growth in all 3 resistant models: intrinsic, induced, and acquired resistance (P < 0.05 vs. controls). No severe toxicity was observed. Conclusion: 211At-trastuzumab demonstrates potent antitumor efficacy against trastuzumab-resistant HER2-positive USC in preclinical models. Targeted α-therapy may represent a promising strategy to overcome resistance to HER2-targeted therapy.

42951680.label: Background
42951680.text: Prostate Imaging Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS) 3 lesions often undergo biopsy despite a low positive predictive value (< 25%) for clinically significant prostate cancer (csPCa), defined as International Society of Urological Pathology (ISUP) Grade Group ≥ 2.

42951680.label: Purpose
42951680.text: To determine whether mean apparent diffusion coefficient (mADC), alone or with prostate-specific antigen (PSA)-based metrics, improves zone-specific PI-RADS 3 classification for csPCa detection.

42951680.label: Population
42951680.text: One hunderd and seventy-one males (71 ± 8 years) with 191 PI-RADS 3 lesions who underwent multiparametric MRI and targeted biopsy.

42951680.label: Field strength/sequence
42951680.text: 3 T, T2-weighted turbo spin-echo imaging, single-shot echo-planar diffusion-weighted imaging, and fat-suppressed dynamic contrast-enhanced T1-weighted gradient echo sequences.

42951680.label: Assessment
42951680.text: mADC, PSA, PSA density (PSAD), prostate volume, and body mass index were analyzed.

42951680.label: Statistical tests
42951680.text: Logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analyses assessed associations with malignancy and diagnostic performance.

42951680.label: Results
42951680.text: mADC was significantly lower in cancers than non-cancers in 133 PZ lesions (885 ± 165 vs. 1068 ± 168 × 10-6 mm2/s) and 58 TZ lesions (670 ± 127 vs. 832 ± 179 × 10-6 mm2/s). In the PZ, mADC alone, and with PSAD showed no significantly different area under the curve (AUC, 0.79 vs. 0.80, p = 0.28). A combination of mADC and PSAD would result in hypothetical estimated lesion-level biopsy avoidance. In the TZ, combining mADC with PSAD yielded significantly higher AUC than mADC alone (0.88 vs. 0.77, difference: 0.109 [95% CI: 0.010-0.208]). This combination would result in hypothetical estimated lesion-level biopsy avoidance in 58 of 82 non-cancers (71%) while missing one csPCa in the PZ, and 27 of 35 noncancerous lesions while missing one csPCa in TZ.

42951680.label: Data conclusion
42951680.text: mADC combined with PSAD showed a significant increase in discrimination in the TZ, suggesting improved PI-RADS 3 stratification; independent validation is required before clinical implementation.

43007080.text: Background Gadolinium retention in bone after gadolinium-based contrast agent (GBCA) exposure is documented in adults but unquantified in children, who may have higher cumulative doses from early imaging. Purpose To quantify and compare residual gadolinium in pediatric bone tissue after macrocyclic and linear GBCA exposure. Materials and Methods In this prospective pilot study, individuals under 18 years of age scheduled for median sternotomy who had undergone clinically indicated GBCA-enhanced or unenhanced MRI were included between January 2018 and August 2024 at a single academic medical center and categorized into three groups: linear GBCA exposed (gadobenate), macrocyclic GBCA exposed (gadoterate), and control (no GBCA exposure). Bone samples were obtained during surgery and analyzed for gadolinium concentration (micrograms of gadolinium per gram of bone tissue). Linear regression modeling was used to analyze the impact of GBCA exposure on bone gadolinium concentration. Results A total of 29 individuals were included: nine exposed to linear GBCA (median age, 12.0 years [IQR, 4.0-14.0 years]; five male individuals), 11 exposed to macrocyclic GBCA (median age, 13.0 years [IQR, 3.3-14.8 years]; eight male individuals), and nine control individuals (median age, 1.8 years [IQR, 0.5-6.3 years]; seven male individuals). Gadolinium was detected in bone tissue in all groups. Median bone gadolinium concentrations were 0.001 μg/g (IQR, 0.0007-0.0015 μg/g) with no GBCA exposure, 0.007 μg/g (IQR, 0.004-0.011 μg/g) with gadoterate exposure, and 0.141 μg/g (IQR, 0.079-0.374 μg/g) with gadobenate exposure. GBCA exposure was associated with gadolinium concentration (adjusted R2 = 0.77; P < .001). Gadobenate exposure was associated with higher gadolinium concentrations than no GBCA exposure (lnβ [log-transformed regression coefficient] = 4.9 [95% CI: 3.7, 5.9]; fold change, 129.8; P < .001) and gadoterate exposure (lnβ = 2.8 [95% CI: 1.6, 3.8]; fold change, 16.0; P < .001). Gadoterate exposure was also associated with higher gadolinium concentrations than no GBCA exposure (lnβ = 2.1 [95% CI: 1.5, 2.7]; fold change, 8.1; P < .001). Conclusion Exposure to the linear agent gadobenate at MRI was associated with higher gadolinium concentrations in bone tissue than no GBCA exposure or exposure to the macrocyclic agent gadoterate; trace gadolinium in the bone tissue of controls may reflect environmental exposure.

43019230.text: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) or scleroderma is a multisystem autoimmune disorder characterized by a variable pattern of skin thickening and involvement of visceral organs. The pathophysiology is similar across all organs, which is chronic low-grade inflammation, with vasculopathy and eventual fibrosis. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, particularly in patients with established disease comprising characteristic skin and visceral manifestations, with a supportive role of laboratory and imaging findings. The presence of radiologic signs such as hidebound bowel or a combination of patulous lower esophageal sphincter, pulmonary fibrosis, skin thickening, and Raynaud phenomenon is relatively specific for SSc. Nevertheless, imaging in SSc is primarily used to determine the pattern, severity, and complications of visceral organ involvement, rather than for diagnosis of SSc. Radiologic evaluation in SSc employs a wide gamut of investigations, depending on the organ of interest. For example, US is used for the skin and superficial tissues; fluoroscopy, CT, or MR enterography for the gastrointestinal tract; endoanal US or MRI for the internal anal sphincter; high-resolution CT for the lungs; echocardiography and cardiac MRI for SSc-related pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) and cardiac disease; and radiography, CT, or MRI for musculoskeletal involvement. Early diagnosis of treatable features, such as PAH and gastroesophageal reflux, can help reduce the morbidity and mortality associated with SSc. Imaging is additionally useful to prognosticate and monitor the disease. The authors focus on the multisystem, multimodality imaging manifestations of SSc with relevant differential diagnoses to bridge the gaps in knowledge about SSc.

43033330.label: Objectives
43033330.text: To assess performance and agreement of a commercial artificial intelligence (AI) tool relative to routine pediatric radiologists' bone age assessments in a large pediatric cohort, with focus on different groups of growth disorders.

43033330.label: Materials and methods
43033330.text: One thousand five hundred sixteen anterior-posterior hand radiographs of pediatric patients (50.6% boys, mean age 10.84 ± 3.66 years) were retrospectively analyzed using the AI tool BoneAge. AI results were compared with board-certified pediatric radiologists' reports using Bland-Altman plots, Spearman correlations, and the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Subgroup analyses were performed for three major indications: genetic/neuroendocrine (n = 1179), orthopedic (n = 152), and oncologic disorders (n = 185).

43033330.label: Results
43033330.text: Mean absolute difference (MAD) in estimated bone age by radiologists and AI was 6.4 ± 7.0 months for the whole cohort, with complete concordance in 45.1% of cases. Best results were achieved in orthopedic questions with an MAD of 4.1 ± 5.6 months (genetic/neuroendocrine: 6.6 ± 7.2, oncologic: 6.7 ± 6.3 months). There was significant correlation between AI and radiologists for the whole study population (ρ = 0.980), and the three main groups: genetic/neuroendocrine (ρ = 0.974), orthopedic (ρ = 0.952), and oncologic indications (ρ = 0.988). ICCs for the entire cohort and the main indication groups were > 0.9, indicating excellent agreement between radiologist and AI.

43033330.label: Conclusion
43033330.text: The investigated algorithm showed good agreement with bone age assessments performed by pediatric radiologists in a large pediatric cohort. Novel to previous studies, the indication for imaging was considered, demonstrating that agreement between algorithm output and radiologists' assessments varied across disease groups, with highest agreement observed in orthopedic indications.

43033330.label: Key points
43033330.text: Question The performance of artificial intelligence tools for bone age assessment among different subgroups of pediatric patients according to underlying diseases has not yet been investigated. Findings Automated bone age assessment reliably correlates with estimation by pediatric radiologists. Software output differs according to disease groups, with best results for orthopedic indications. Critical relevance statement In a real-world scenario, the commercial software showed good agreement with routine bone age assessments in a large cohort of pediatric patients. The observed disease-dependent variation suggests that radiologists should consider disease-specific differences when using additional automated tools.

43043180.text: Background Nationally representative data comparing high-risk benign breast disease (BBD) detection with digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) versus digital mammography are lacking. Purpose To describe temporal trends in high-risk BBD detection rates at screening mammography in the Breast Cancer Surveillance Consortium (BCSC) over nearly 2 decades and to evaluate the association between mammographic modality and high-risk BBD detection. Materials and Methods In this retrospective cohort study using prospectively collected data from the BCSC, screening mammograms obtained from 2005 to 2022 among women aged 40 to 79 years at 97 health care facilities were analyzed; examinations in women with prior breast cancer or mastectomy were excluded. Regression analyses were used to estimate annual percent change (APC) in detection rates, and multivariable logistic regression was used to estimate adjusted odds ratios (ORs) according to mammographic modality. Results A total of 4 469 664 screening mammograms in 1 190 380 women (mean age, 57.3 years ± 10.1 [SD]) were included. The overall high-risk BBD detection rate was 1.11 per 1000 examinations, with no evidence of a temporal trend since 2017 (APC = 5.3% [95% CI: -1.1, 21.9]; P = .09). Atypical ductal hyperplasia detection declined from 2009 to 2017 (APC = -7.4% [95% CI: -12.0, -5.4]; P < .001). Detection of radial sclerosing lesions (APC = 5.4% [95% CI: 3.5, 7.8]; P < .001) and atypical papillary lesions (APC = 19.0% [95% CI: 14.8, 25.1]; P < .001) increased from 2005 to 2022. Compared with digital mammography, DBT was associated with increased detection of high-risk BBD overall (OR = 1.36 [95% CI: 1.24, 1.49]; P < .001), lobular carcinoma in situ (OR = 1.37 [95% CI: 1.02, 1.85]; P = .04), atypical lobular hyperplasia (OR = 1.45 [95% CI: 1.19, 1.77]; P < .001), and radial sclerosing lesions (OR = 2.64 [95% CI: 2.15, 3.23]; P < .001). Conclusion Over the past 2 decades, detection of atypical papillary lesions and radial sclerosing lesions increased, whereas detection of atypical ductal hyperplasia declined. DBT was associated with increased detection of high-risk BBD, including lobular carcinoma in situ, atypical lobular hyperplasia, and radial sclerosing lesions.

43057880.text: Personalized radiopharmaceutical therapies rely on accurate and reproducible absorbed dose estimates. However, substantial variability persists because of differences in imaging protocols, segmentation, time-activity curve fitting and integration, and dose calculation implementation. The Society of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging 177Lu Dosimetry Challenge was a 5-task international study designed to isolate sources of variability in image-based dosimetry workflows. In this final publication, we integrate findings across the series and perform a retrospective analysis of the original full-workflow submissions to estimate the reduction in variability achievable through methodologic consistency and quality assurance. Methods: In this final analysis, the original task 1 end-to-end SPECT/CT workflow submissions were reevaluated to generate a refined task 1 dataset by excluding previously identified processing or reporting mistakes, as well as submissions with methodologic choices inconsistent with the recommendations derived from the challenge. Exclusion criteria included nonstandard volume-of-interest (VOI) definitions, inconsistent VOI handling, inappropriate time-activity curve fitting and integration, and omission of required mass scaling. Variability was quantified using the interquartile range and quartile coefficient of dispersion (QCD). Results: The refined task 1 analysis showed that a substantial fraction of the observed variability is potentially avoidable. Exclusions reduced the analyzed dataset by approximately 50% and narrowed absorbed dose distributions for most organs and lesions. For patient A, QCD decreased for total kidney (23.1% to 3.0%), spleen (24.2% to 7.8%), and lesion 1 (22.8% to 13.3%). For patient B, organ variability also decreased (12.6% to 8.2% in the liver and 15.3% to 10.9% in the left kidney), although variability for some lesions decreased less substantially. Findings across the challenge indicated that, among the workflow steps evaluated, segmentation and time-activity curve fitting/integration were the dominant contributors to variability, whereas variability from the absorbed dose calculation step alone was generally small once upstream inputs were standardized. Conclusion: A substantial portion of variability in radiopharmaceutical therapy dosimetry is potentially avoidable through standardization and quality assurance. Under more standardized conditions, organ absorbed dose estimates showed markedly lower variability, with QCD values as low as 3%. These results support implementation of standardized VOI segmentation rules, time-activity curve modeling conventions, and auditable quality control and reporting procedures to improve reproducibility in both clinical trials and routine practice.

43076930.label: Purpose
43076930.text: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) disrupts multi-organ glucose metabolism, but systemic inter-organ metabolic coordination and its relevance to cognition remain insufficiently characterized. This study aimed to construct whole-body metabolic covariance networks using whole-body 18F-FDG PET/MR and explore their associations with cognitive performance in T2DM.

43076930.label: Methods
43076930.text: Twenty-nine patients with T2DM and 46 healthy controls were enrolled. Mean standardized uptake value normalized to lean body mass (SULmean) were extracted from nine cerebral subregions and nine peripheral tissue compartments to calculate whole-body metabolic covariance. These 18 regions were then aggregated into nine major nodes to construct the metabolic connectivity network. Two brain-peripheral decoupling scores were derived from Z-residual covariance features. Correlation and mediation analyses assessed associations between brain-peripheral decoupling and cognition, while four predictive models were compared for classification performance.

43076930.label: Results
43076930.text: Although intra-brain metabolic correlations were numerically higher in T2DM patients than in controls across 32 of 36 region pairs, these differences did not survive FDR correction (all q > 0.05). Similarly, brain-peripheral couplings showed only nominal differences between groups and were not FDR-significant (q > 0.05). Network topology analysis indicated different descriptive hub configurations (spleen and pancreas in controls vs. subcutaneous (SAT) and visceral adipose tissue (VAT) in T2DM). Across all participants, the signed decoupling score showed a modest inverse association with MoCA scores in the pooled cohort (r = - 0.31, P = 0.007) that did not reach significance within either subgroup (T2DM: r = - 0.14, P = 0.445). Mediation analysis provided no statistical evidence that brain-peripheral decoupling mediates the association between T2DM status and cognitive outcomes. The multimodal ElasticNet model achieved the highest classification performance (AUC = 0.726, 95% CI 0.602-0.840).

43076930.label: Conclusions
43076930.text: Whole-body metabolic network analysis may provide complementary systems-level information for characterizing T2DM-related metabolic dysregulation and cognitive vulnerability.
